title: Ezekiel 43:13–17
context: The LORD gives the measurements of the altar, using a cubit that is a cubit and a hand width. The altar rises in stages from a base with a border, through a lower ledge and a greater ledge, to an upper altar with a hearth twelve cubits square and four horns, and its steps face east. The meaning of some terms, including the words rendered hearth and horns, and the exact shape of the stages are discussed by interpreters. Both traditions read the list as part of the same vision of ordered, holy worship, and neither turns its measurements into a point of contrast.

verses.text: “These are the measurements of the altar by cubits (the cubit is a cubit and a hand width): the bottom shall be a cubit, and the width a cubit, and its border around its edge a span; and this shall be the base of the altar.
verses.arminianNotes: These are the measurements of the altar by cubits Arminian readers find the altar described with care, beginning from its base and the border around its edge, a span wide.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the long cubit, a cubit and a hand width, is the same unit used in 40:5. The measurements are given precisely without being made into a point of debate.

verses.text: From the bottom on the ground to the lower ledge shall be two cubits, and the width one cubit; and from the lesser ledge to the greater ledge shall be four cubits, and the width a cubit.
verses.arminianNotes: From the bottom on the ground to the lower ledge shall be two cubits, Arminian readers see the altar rising in stages, from a lower ledge to a greater ledge, each with its own dimensions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the stepped design is difficult to reconstruct exactly. The rising levels seem to express the altar’s importance at the very center of the community’s worship.

verses.text: The upper altar shall be four cubits; and from the altar hearth and upward there shall be four horns.
verses.arminianNotes: The upper altar shall be four cubits; Arminian readers see the hearth as the place where offerings were burned, with four horns rising from it, recalling the horns of the altar in Exodus 27:2.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the terms rendered upper altar, hearth, and horns are discussed by interpreters, and their exact sense is uncertain. The horns appear again in the consecration rite of 43:20.

verses.text: The altar hearth shall be twelve cubits long by twelve wide, square in its four sides.
verses.arminianNotes: The altar hearth shall be twelve cubits long by twelve wide, square in its four sides. Arminian readers take the square shape as a mark of order and completeness in the vision of worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the altar is far larger than the bronze altar of Exodus 27:1, which was five cubits square. The difference is named without being harmonized.

verses.text: The ledge shall be fourteen cubits long by fourteen wide in its four sides; and the border about it shall be half a cubit; and its bottom shall be a cubit around; and its steps shall look toward the east.”
verses.arminianNotes: The ledge shall be fourteen cubits long by fourteen wide Arminian readers see the final measurements of the ledge and border, completing the description of the altar.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the steps of the altar shall look toward the east. The orientation matches the east gate through which the glory entered in 43:4.
